region.text: Liège and the county of Huy

ledger.note: 980: the bishops become princes. The infobox dates the 'acquisition of secular powers' to 980; the Notker page: he 'received the countship of Huy' in 980 and became 'the first prince-bishop'. The Liège page's text says only that the bishops received lordship over Huy 'in the 10th century'. The page gives no border.

region.text: Haspinga (Haspengouw) around Borgloon; the page says its extent is disputed

ledger.note: 1040: Henry III's charter 'granted this county to the Cathedral of Saint-Lambert'. The county was 'Haspinga'; its extent is disputed and may have included part of Loon (Loon page). The circle is only an indication.

region.text: the lordship of Bouillon in the Ardennes

ledger.note: 1096: Liège buys Bouillon. 'In 1095, Godfrey of Bouillon sold Bouillon to Otbert, the Prince-Bishop of Liège' to fund the First Crusade (body); a footnote and the Liège infobox give 1096. [Reviewer eu-08-x, 2026-10-25: counterpart set to duchy-of-lower-lorraine, whose ledger carries the matching 1096 loss of Bouillon (Godfrey was duke of Lower Lorraine)]

region.text: the county of Loon, which corresponded approximately with the modern Belgian province of Limburg

ledger.note: By 1190 Loon is under the bishop. 'By 1190 the count had come under the bishop's overlordship' (Loon page); in 1179 Rudolf of Zähringen's campaign had devastated Borgloon.

1213: Moha annexed. Albert II of Dagsburg, the last count of Moha, died without a son in 1212; Henry I of Brabant and Louis II of Loon both claimed it. After the battle of Steppes on 13 October 1213 'Moha was annexed to Liège'. [Reviewer eu-08-x, 2026-10-25: confidence lowered to 2: the Battle of Steppes page says 'Moha was annexed to Liège' without a year; 1213 is inferred from the battle of 13 October 1213]

region.text: the county of Loon, which corresponded approximately with the modern Belgian province of Limburg

ledger.note: 1362: Engelbert III seizes Loon. The comital line died out in 1336 and the estates went to the lords of Heinsberg with the bishop's consent; 'in 1362 Prince-Bishop Engelbert III of the Marck nevertheless seized Loon'. Arnold VI of Rumigny held the title and later 'renounced in favour of Liege'.

region.text: the county of Loon, which corresponded approximately with the modern Belgian province of Limburg

ledger.note: 1366: Loon incorporated. Engelbert 'finally incorporated it into the Liège territory in 1366'.

It 'remained a separate entity (quartier) within Liège, whose prince-bishops assumed the comital title'; the Liège infobox also dates the annexation to 1366. [Reviewer eu-08-x, 2026-10-25: counterpart strings of the Loon events set to the slug county-of-loon listed in the author's counterparts_needing_dossiers]

region.text: the lordship of Bouillon in the Ardennes

ledger.note: 1551: Henry II of France occupies Bouillon. He held it 1551-1559 'during the Italian War and confirmed Robert IV as Duke'; from 1560 the dukes of Bouillon also ruled Sedan, and 'from 1678 it was a sovereign duchy under French protection' (a footnote has it 'ceded to France in 1678'). The page does not say when Liège's overlordship ended.

wars.name: Rudolf of Zähringen's campaign against Loon

zones.text: Borgloon, the old capital of Loon

wars.outcome: Prince-Bishop Rudolf of Zähringen's campaign 'devastated the county's old capital at Borgloon in 1179'; by 1190 the count was under the bishop's overlordship.

wars.name: War of the Moha succession
wars.outcome: Albert II of Dagsburg died without a son in 1212; Henry I of Brabant and Louis II of Loon both claimed Moha; at Steppes on 13 October 1213 the Liège side (with Loon and Henry III of Limburg) beat the Brabantine army and Moha was annexed to Liège.

wars.name: Annexation of Loon

zones.text: the county of Loon, which corresponded approximately with the modern Belgian province of Limburg

wars.outcome: Engelbert III seized Loon in 1362; Arnold VI of Rumigny renounced in favour of Liège and Engelbert incorporated it in 1366.

wars.name: La Marck war over Liège and Bouillon

zones.text: the lordship of Bouillon in the Ardennes

wars.outcome: William de La Marck ordered the assassination of Bishop Louis de Bourbon in 1482 and John of Hornes was elected; the Treaty of Tongeren of 21 May 1484 ended the war, the La Marcks gave up their claim on Liège and kept Bouillon Castle as a pledge for a 30,000-livre loan.

wars.name: Liège Revolution
wars.outcome: The revolution began on 18 August 1789 and the prince-bishop Hoensbroeck left on 26-27 August; Prussians occupied Liège from November 1789 to April 1790; Austrian forces entered on 12 January 1791 (the page also has 12 February) and Hoensbroeck regained power.

notes: Six pages opened (one over the 2-5 budget, because the state lived 815 years). The pages give no area and no border: the 30 km circle round Liège is the researcher's reading of the core; the final form 'included most of the present Belgian provinces of Liège and Limburg' (main page), and the page does not date the growth of the Liège province part. Not settled: the Burgundian period of 1468-1477 (the page names the pillage of the episcopal city in the 15th century only; the page for the sack failed to load), the Haspinga extent, the date and manner of the end of Liège's hold on Bouillon (1551/1559 against a footnote of 1678), the Bouillon sale year (1095 against 1096), the 1791 return date (12 January against 12 February), and the Horne terms. The Liège page says the diocese was larger than the princedom until 1559; the diocese is not drawn. Needs dossiers or counterpart slugs: County of Loon, County of Moha (small), Duchy of Bouillon (1095-1795).
